topics.title: Mole Concept & Stoichiometry
topics.notes:
The mole is chemistry's bridge between the microscopic (individual atoms and molecules) and the macroscopic (grams you can weigh on a scale). One mole of anything contains Avogadro's number of particles: 6.022×10²³. Molar mass (grams per mole) is the conversion factor that lets you move between mass and moles: moles = mass/molar mass.

Empirical formula problems give you percent composition and ask for the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. The method is always the same: convert each percentage to moles (treating percentages as grams per 100g of compound), then divide every mole value by the smallest one to get a ratio, and if needed, multiply through by a small whole number to clear any remaining fractions. The molecular formula is then just the empirical formula scaled up by whatever whole-number multiplier makes the mass match the given molecular weight.

For gas-phase compounds specifically, you can find molar mass without ever weighing a solid sample: PM=ρRT (a rearranged ideal gas law, where ρ is density) connects a gas's density directly to its molar mass. This shows up constantly in past questions asking for molar mass given only density, temperature, and pressure.

KEY FORMULA: moles = mass/molar mass, and for gases, M = ρRT/P.

topics.title: Gas Laws
topics.notes:
The ideal gas law, PV=nRT, is the single formula that unifies Boyle's Law (P∝1/V at constant T), Charles's Law (V∝T at constant P), and Avogadro's Law (V∝n at constant P,T) into one relationship. Most gas-law problems are really just PV=nRT solved for whichever variable is missing — the skill is correctly identifying what's held constant and what's changing.

When conditions change from one state to another (not looking for an absolute value, just how things shift), the combined gas law is faster: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂. Temperature must always be in Kelvin for this to work — using Celsius directly is the single most common error in this topic.

Dalton's Law of partial pressures says that in a mixture of gases, each gas contributes to the total pressure in proportion to how much of it (moles, or equivalently mole fraction) is present: P_gas = (mole fraction of that gas) × P_total. This is why 'partial pressure' questions always start by finding mole fractions.

Graham's Law describes how gases of different molar masses move (effuse or diffuse) at different rates: lighter gases move faster. Specifically, rate ∝ 1/√(molar mass), which means TIME to effuse a given amount is proportional to √(molar mass) — heavier gases take longer.

KEY FORMULA: PV = nRT (R = 0.0821 L·atm/mol·K).

topics.title: Atomic Structure & Electron Configuration
topics.notes:
An atom's identity is fixed by its number of protons (atomic number, Z) — this never changes without changing the element itself. Neutrons add mass without changing identity (isotopes), and electrons determine charge: a neutral atom has electrons equal to protons; an ion has gained or lost electrons, shifting that balance.

Electron configuration follows a filling order (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, ...) based on increasing energy, with each subshell holding a specific maximum: s-subshells hold 2 electrons, p-subshells hold 6, d-subshells hold 10. A handful of elements — chromium and copper are the classic examples — deviate from the 'expected' configuration because a half-filled or fully-filled d-subshell is unusually stable, so electrons rearrange to achieve that even though it looks like it 'shouldn't' happen by the simple filling rules.

Quantum numbers describe an electron's specific state: n (principal, energy level, 1,2,3...), l (angular momentum/subshell shape, 0 to n−1), mₗ (orbital orientation, −l to +l), and mₛ (spin, +½ or −½). Past questions testing 'which set is impossible' are checking whether l and mₗ actually respect these range rules for the given n.

KEY IDEA: protons define the element; neutrons define the isotope; electrons (relative to protons) define the charge.

topics.title: Chemical Bonding & Molecular Geometry
topics.notes:
Every single bond is one sigma bond. Every double bond is one sigma plus one pi bond. Every triple bond is one sigma plus two pi bonds. This is the entire foundation for counting sigma and pi bonds in any molecule — count every bond in the structure once as sigma, then add one pi for each 'extra' bond in a double, and two pi for each triple.

Hybridization describes how an atom mixes its orbitals to form bonds, and it's directly determined by how many things (bonding groups + lone pairs) surround the central atom: 2 groups → sp (linear), 3 groups → sp² (trigonal planar), 4 groups → sp³ (tetrahedral), 5 groups → sp³d (trigonal bipyramidal), 6 groups → sp³d² (octahedral). Count the groups around the atom in question, and the hybridization follows directly.

The octet rule (atoms 'want' 8 electrons around them) is a useful guideline, not an absolute law — past questions specifically test the exceptions. Electron-deficient atoms (like boron or aluminum in compounds such as BF₃ or AlI₃) may stop at 6 electrons. Hypervalent atoms (like phosphorus in PCl₅ or sulfur in SF₆) can exceed 8, because elements from period 3 onward have accessible d-orbitals that let them accommodate more bonding pairs.

KEY IDEA: count the groups around an atom to get hybridization; count bond types (single/double/triple) to get sigma/pi totals.

topics.title: The Periodic Table & Periodic Trends
topics.notes:
The periodic table is organized so that elements in the same column (group) share similar chemical behavior, because they have the same number of valence (outermost) electrons. Moving across a period (left to right), atomic radius shrinks and electronegativity rises, because each added proton pulls the same outer shell in tighter without adding a new shell. Moving down a group, atomic radius grows and electronegativity falls, since each row adds a whole new electron shell farther from the nucleus.

Metalloids sit along the 'staircase' line running diagonally through the table (boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium) — they show properties intermediate between metals and nonmetals, which is exactly why past questions test recognizing them specifically rather than lumping them with either category.

Oxide behavior follows a predictable pattern tied to position on the table: metal oxides (especially from the left side) tend to be basic, nonmetal oxides (right side) tend to be acidic, and oxides near the metalloid staircase are often amphoteric (react as both an acid and a base depending on what they're paired with). Physical state also varies systematically — most oxides of highly electronegative nonmetal elements in high oxidation states, like N₂O₅, are solids, while lower-oxidation-state versions like NO and N₂O are gases.

KEY IDEA: across a period, radius shrinks and electronegativity rises; down a group, the reverse.

topics.title: Nuclear Chemistry
topics.notes:
Radioactive decay is a random process at the level of any single atom, but wildly predictable in bulk: a fixed fraction of any radioactive sample decays in a fixed amount of time, called the half-life (t½). After one half-life, half the original amount remains; after two half-lives, a quarter remains; after three, an eighth — each half-life cuts the remaining amount in half again, regardless of how much was there to start.

For whole-number multiples of the half-life, you can just repeatedly halve the starting amount — no calculator needed. For any other elapsed time, the general decay equation is needed: N = N₀×e^(−λt), or equivalently t = t½×ln(N₀/N)/ln(2). This second form is what radiocarbon dating (and similar 'how old is this sample' problems) actually uses — you're given the ratio of remaining to original amount, and solving for t tells you how much time has passed.

Carbon-14 dating specifically works because living organisms constantly exchange carbon with the atmosphere, maintaining a roughly constant ¹⁴C ratio while alive. Once an organism dies, that exchange stops, and the ¹⁴C it already contains simply decays at its known half-life (5,730 years) — measuring how much is left tells you how long ago the organism died.

KEY FORMULA: t = t½ × ln(N₀/N) / ln(2).
